questions.stem: How many grammatical genders do French nouns have?
questions.explanation: Every French noun is either masculine or feminine, including objects with no natural gender — « le livre » is masculine and « la table » feminine for no reason you can reason out. Learn the article with the noun.

questions.stem: Which article goes with a feminine singular noun?
questions.explanation: « La » is the feminine singular 'the'; « le » is masculine singular and « les » is plural for both. « Un » is an indefinite article, a different job entirely.

questions.stem: What is the plural definite article in French?
questions.explanation: « Les » covers both genders in the plural, which makes it the easiest article to use. « L' » is what « le » or « la » become before a vowel, so it is still singular.

questions.stem: Why is it « l'école » rather than « la école »?
options: The noun starts with a vowel
questions.explanation: French avoids two vowel sounds colliding, so « le » and « la » both shorten to « l' » before a vowel or a silent h. It is a sound rule, not a gender rule — « école » is still feminine.

questions.stem: How do you usually make a French noun plural in writing?
questions.explanation: Most nouns add -s, as in English. The catch is that the -s is usually silent, so plural is often heard only in the article: « le livre » and « les livres » sound different at the start, not the end.

questions.stem: Where do most French adjectives go?
options: At the start of the sentence
At the end of the sentence
questions.explanation: « Une voiture rouge », not 'une rouge voiture'. A small group does come first — beau, nouveau, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, bon, mauvais — and those are the exceptions worth memorising.

questions.stem: What does « je » mean?
questions.explanation: « Je » is I. The full set is worth learning in order: je, tu, il/elle, nous, vous, ils/elles — verb endings are taught against that sequence.

questions.stem: What is the difference between « tu » and « vous »?
options: « Tu » is present tense and « vous » is past tense
« Tu » is used in writing and « vous » only in speech
« Tu » is informal or singular; « vous » is formal or plural
« Tu » is masculine and « vous » is feminine
questions.explanation: English lost this distinction centuries ago, so it has to be learned rather than translated. Using « tu » with a stranger or a teacher can read as rude, so when unsure, « vous » is the safe choice.

questions.stem: What is the infinitive ending of « parler »?
questions.explanation: French verbs fall into three groups by infinitive ending: -er, -ir and -re. The -er group is by far the largest and the most regular, which is why it is always taught first.

questions.stem: How do you make a French sentence negative?
options: Add « ne » at the end of the sentence
Put « ne » before the verb and « pas » after it
questions.explanation: French negation is a sandwich: « je ne comprends pas ». English uses one word, French uses two around the verb. In casual speech the « ne » is often dropped, but it belongs in anything written.

questions.stem: Which form of « parler » completes « Je ___ français » ?
questions.explanation: For -er verbs with « je », the -er is replaced by -e. « Parles » is the « tu » form and « parlons » is « nous ». Leaving the infinitive « parler » unchanged is the commonest beginner error.

questions.stem: Which form of « parler » completes « Nous ___ à l'école » ?
questions.explanation: The « nous » ending for -er verbs is -ons, giving « parlons ». « Parlez » goes with « vous » and « parlent » with « ils » — the endings are the whole point of learning the pronoun order.

questions.stem: Which form of « avoir » completes « Tu ___ un chien » ?
questions.explanation: « Avoir » is irregular and must be memorised: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont. « A » without the s is the « il » form, and that missing letter is the usual slip.

questions.stem: Which form of « être » completes « Elle ___ française » ?
questions.explanation: « Être » is the other essential irregular verb: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont. « Es » belongs to « tu » and is the near-miss here.

questions.stem: Which is the correct feminine form of « petit »?
questions.explanation: Most adjectives add -e for the feminine, and that added e makes the final consonant sound — « petit » ends in a silent t, « petite » does not. « Petits » is the masculine plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Adjectives agree in both gender and number, so a feminine plural noun needs -es on the adjective. Each wrong option breaks exactly one rule: no agreement, wrong verb, or a missing plural on the noun.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I am going to eat' using the near future?
questions.explanation: The near future is « aller » plus an infinitive, exactly like English 'going to'. « Je mangerai » is the simple future, a different tense taught later, and « j'ai mangé » is the past.

questions.stem: Which question means 'Do you have a pen?' (informal)?
questions.explanation: Inversion puts the verb before the pronoun and joins them with a hyphen. The second option is a statement without inversion; the third uses « être » instead of « avoir », which would ask if you *are* a pen.

questions.stem: What does « il y a » mean?
questions.explanation: « Il y a » is a fixed expression and does not change for plural: « il y a un livre » and « il y a trois livres » both use it. Translating it word for word gives nonsense, so learn it whole.

questions.stem: Which possessive means 'my' before a feminine singular noun?
questions.explanation: « Mon » is masculine, « ma » feminine, « mes » plural. French possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner — « sa voiture » is 'his car' or 'her car' depending only on context.

questions.stem: Which form of « prendre » completes « Vous ___ le train » ?
questions.explanation: « Prendre » is irregular: je prends, tu prends, il prend, nous prenons, vous prenez, ils prennent. The « vous » ending -ez is regular even in an otherwise irregular verb, which is a useful anchor.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I do not have a brother'?
options: Je ai ne pas de frère
Je ne ai pas un frère
questions.explanation: Two rules combine. « Ne » becomes « n' » before a vowel, and after a negative the indefinite article « un » changes to « de ». That second rule is the one almost everyone misses first time.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'She is going to buy the blue dress'?
options: Elle va acheter la robe bleue
Elle va acheter la bleue robe
Elle va achète la robe bleue
Elle vas acheter la robe bleu
questions.explanation: Three things must hold at once: the adjective follows the noun, the near future takes an infinitive after « aller », and « bleue » agrees with the feminine « robe ». Each wrong option breaks one of the three.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Nous ne avons pas de voiture
Nous avons ne pas de voiture
questions.explanation: The indefinite article becomes « de » after a negative, « ne » elides before the vowel in « avons », and the negative wraps the verb. All three rules apply to the same short sentence.

questions.stem: Why does « une femme heureuse » use « heureuse » rather than « heureux »?
options: It follows the noun rather than preceding it
The adjective agrees with the feminine noun
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -eux take -euse in the feminine, a regular pattern seen in sérieux/sérieuse and dangereux/dangereuse. Position in the sentence has nothing to do with the ending.

questions.stem: Which correctly says 'they (all girls) are French'?
questions.explanation: « Elles » is used when every member of the group is feminine, and both the verb and the adjective must follow. A single male in the group would make it « ils sont français » — a rule worth knowing exists.

questions.stem: In « Je me lève à sept heures », why is « me » there?
options: The verb is reflexive, so the action returns to the subject
It is the object of the sentence
It marks the sentence as a question
questions.explanation: Reflexive verbs describe something done to oneself, and French marks that with a pronoun English usually omits: « se lever » is literally 'to raise oneself'. Daily-routine verbs are mostly of this kind.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct partitive article for 'I eat bread'?
questions.explanation: The partitive « du » means 'some' for an uncountable masculine noun. « Le pain » would mean bread in general or one specific loaf, and « un pain » counts a whole loaf — all grammatical, all saying something else.

questions.stem: Which indefinite article goes with a masculine singular noun?
questions.explanation: « Un » is 'a' with a masculine noun and « une » with a feminine one. « Des » is the plural 'some', and « du » is the partitive for an amount of something uncountable.

questions.stem: What does « des » mean in « J'ai des amis »?
questions.explanation: « Des » is the plural indefinite article, 'some'. English usually leaves it out — 'I have friends' — but French never does, which is why it is so easy to forget.

questions.stem: How do you make « le livre » plural?
questions.explanation: Both the article and the noun change: « le » becomes « les » and the noun takes an -s. Changing only one of the two is the usual slip.

questions.stem: What is the plural of « le gateau »?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in -eau take -x rather than -s in the plural. The sound does not change, so this is a spelling rule you only meet in writing.

questions.stem: What is the plural of « le journal »?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in -al usually change to -aux: « animal » gives « animaux », « cheval » gives « chevaux ». This one you can hear, unlike most French plurals.

questions.stem: Which word means 'I' in French?
questions.explanation: « Je » is 'I'. « Tu » is informal 'you', « il » is 'he' or 'it', and « on » is the everyday 'we' or a general 'one'.

questions.stem: What does « nous » mean?
questions.explanation: « Nous » is 'we', though in speech « on » does the same job far more often — « on y va » rather than « nous y allons ».

questions.stem: Why does « on » take the same verb ending as « il » and « elle »?
options: It has no verb form of its own
It is grammatically third person singular
questions.explanation: « On » often means 'we' but it behaves as a singular third person, so it is « on va » and never « on vont ». Meaning and grammar pull in different directions here.

questions.stem: Which form of « aimer » completes « Il ___ le chocolat » ?
questions.explanation: The « il » form of an -er verb drops -er and adds -e. « Aimes » is for « tu », « aiment » for « ils », and « aimez » for « vous ».

questions.stem: Which form of « habiter » completes « Vous ___ a Melbourne » ?
questions.explanation: « Vous » takes -ez on every regular -er verb. « Habitons » belongs to « nous » and « habitent » to « ils » or « elles ».

questions.stem: Which form of « finir » completes « Nous ___ a midi » ?
questions.explanation: Regular -ir verbs add -iss- before the plural endings: nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent. Dropping the -iss- is the standard error.

questions.stem: Which form of « vendre » completes « Elle ___ des fleurs » ?
questions.explanation: Regular -re verbs have no ending at all in the third person singular: the stem stands alone. « Vends » is the « je » and « tu » form.

questions.stem: Which form of « aller » completes « Je ___ au cinema » ?
questions.explanation: « Aller » is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. Almost nothing about it looks like the infinitive.

questions.stem: Which form of « faire » completes « Nous ___ nos devoirs » ?
questions.explanation: « Nous faisons » is regular in shape even though the verb is irregular. « Faites » is the « vous » form and one of the odder ones in French.

questions.stem: Which form of « venir » completes « Ils ___ demain » ?
questions.explanation: « Venir » doubles the n in the third person plural: ils viennent. The singular forms use one n — il vient.

questions.stem: Where do « ne » and « pas » go around a verb?
options: pas before the verb, ne after it
ne before the verb, pas after it
questions.explanation: Negation wraps the verb: « je ne mange pas ». In speech the « ne » is often dropped, but it is always written.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I never eat fish'?
options: Je ne mange jamais de poisson
Je ne mange pas jamais de poisson
Je ne jamais mange de poisson
questions.explanation: « Jamais » replaces « pas » in the wrapper rather than joining it, and the partitive « du » collapses to « de » after a negative.

questions.stem: Why does « J'ai un chien » become « Je n'ai pas de chien »?
options: Un is never used with animals
The article changes to de after a negative
questions.explanation: After a negative, « un », « une », « du », « de la » and « des » all collapse to « de » in front of a direct object. This does not happen after « etre ».

questions.stem: Which is the simplest way to turn « Tu parles francais » into a question?
options: Add a question mark and raise your voice
questions.explanation: Intonation alone makes a question in spoken French, and in writing the question mark does it. « Est-ce que » and inversion are the more formal alternatives.

questions.stem: What does « est-ce que » do to a sentence?
options: Turns a statement into a question
Puts the verb into the past
questions.explanation: « Est-ce que » is a question marker with no English equivalent — it is placed in front of a statement and the word order behind it never changes.

questions.stem: Which question uses correct inversion?
questions.explanation: Inversion swaps the verb and the subject pronoun and joins them with a hyphen. It is the most formal of the three ways to ask.

questions.stem: What does « ou » ask about?
questions.explanation: « Ou » asks where. « Quand » asks when, « pourquoi » asks why and « comment » asks how.

questions.stem: Which question word means 'how many'?
questions.explanation: « Combien » asks how many or how much. « Comment » is how, and the two are easy to confuse because they start the same way.

questions.stem: Which possessive means 'my' before a masculine singular noun?
questions.explanation: « Mon » goes with a masculine noun, « ma » with a feminine one and « mes » with any plural. « Moi » is not a possessive at all.

questions.stem: Why is it « mon amie » even though « amie » is feminine?
options: The noun starts with a vowel
Amie is an exception to gender
questions.explanation: « Ma » would put two vowel sounds together, so French uses « mon » before any noun starting with a vowel regardless of gender. The noun is still feminine.

questions.stem: What happens when « a » meets « le »?
questions.explanation: « A » plus « le » becomes « au », and « a » plus « les » becomes « aux ». With « la » and « l' » there is no contraction.

questions.stem: What happens when « de » meets « les »?
questions.explanation: « De » plus « les » gives « des », and « de » plus « le » gives « du ». This is why « des » looks like an article and a contraction at once.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I go to the cinema'?
questions.explanation: « A le » is never written: it contracts to « au ». The contraction is compulsory, not a stylistic choice.

questions.stem: Which phrase means 'there is' or 'there are'?
questions.explanation: « Il y a » is a fixed phrase meaning there is or there are, and it never changes for number — « il y a un chat » and « il y a trois chats ».

questions.stem: Which is the correct feminine form of « heureux »?
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -eux change to -euse in the feminine. The same pattern gives « serieuse » and « delicieuse ».

questions.stem: Which is the correct feminine form of « blanc »?
questions.explanation: « Blanc » becomes « blanche », one of a small group that changes shape rather than simply adding -e. « Franc » gives « franche » the same way.

questions.stem: Which adjective goes before the noun?
questions.explanation: A short list of very common adjectives — beauty, age, goodness and size — sit before the noun. Colours and nationalities go after.

questions.stem: Which sentence puts the adjective in the usual place?
questions.explanation: Most French adjectives follow the noun, which is the opposite of English and the single most common word-order error at this level.

questions.stem: How do you say 'the big houses'?
questions.explanation: The adjective agrees in both gender and number, so feminine plural takes -es. « Grand » is one of the adjectives that goes before the noun.

questions.stem: Which verb do you use to give your age in French?
questions.explanation: French has years rather than being them: « j'ai quatorze ans ». Saying « je suis quatorze » is the classic English-speaker mistake.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'She is fifteen'?
questions.explanation: Age uses « avoir » and the word « ans » is compulsory — leaving it off is as odd in French as saying 'she has fifteen' would be in English.

questions.stem: Which verb does French use for the weather?
questions.explanation: « Il fait beau », « il fait froid » — weather is something the day does. « Il pleut » and « il neige » are their own verbs.

questions.stem: What does « je voudrais » mean?
questions.explanation: « Je voudrais » is the polite conditional of « vouloir ». « Je veux » means I want and sounds blunt in a shop.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I am going to play' in the near future?
questions.explanation: The near future is « aller » conjugated plus a plain infinitive. The second verb never changes its form.

questions.stem: Which auxiliary does « manger » take in the passe compose?
questions.explanation: Most French verbs form the perfect with « avoir »: « j'ai mange ». A small group of movement verbs and all reflexives take « etre » instead.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I went to the park'?
options: Je suis alle a le parc
questions.explanation: « Aller » is one of the verbs that takes « etre » in the perfect, and « a le » must contract to « au ». Both rules have to hold at once.

questions.stem: What does the « se » in « se laver » tell you?
options: The verb is in the past
The action is done to oneself
questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun sends the action back to the subject: « je me lave » is I wash myself. The pronoun changes with the person.

questions.stem: Which correctly says 'we get up at seven'?
options: Nous nous levons a sept heures
Nous se levons a sept heures
Nous nous lever a sept heures
questions.explanation: The reflexive pronoun matches the subject, so « nous » is followed by « nous ». Seeing the word twice looks wrong and is right.

questions.stem: What is the difference between « c'est » and « il est »?
options: Il est can only describe objects
C'est is used before an article or a name
questions.explanation: « C'est un professeur » but « il est professeur » — with an article or a proper noun you need « c'est », and with a bare job or adjective you need « il est ».

questions.stem: Which word means 'because'?
questions.explanation: « Parce que » answers « pourquoi ». The two look alike and are the question and the answer rather than synonyms.

questions.stem: How do you say 'a lot of homework'?
questions.explanation: Expressions of quantity take plain « de » with no article: beaucoup de, un peu de, assez de, trop de.

questions.stem: Which sentence says 'I am taller than my brother'?
options: Je suis plus grand mon frere
Je suis le plus grand que mon frere
Je suis plus grand que mon frere
Je suis plus grand de mon frere
questions.explanation: Comparisons use « plus ... que ». Swapping in « de » is an error carried over from other languages.

questions.stem: What does « moins » mean in a comparison?
questions.explanation: « Plus » is more, « moins » is less and « aussi ... que » is as ... as. All three use « que » for the second half.

questions.stem: Which pronoun would you use to address your teacher?
questions.explanation: « Vous » is the polite singular as well as the plural. Using « tu » with an adult you do not know is a real discourtesy, not just a grammar slip.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'there are no books'?
options: Il y a pas de livres
Il n'y a pas les livres
Il n'y a pas de livres
Il n'y a pas des livres
questions.explanation: « Il y a » wraps in « ne ... pas » like any verb, and the article after the negative collapses to « de ».

questions.stem: Where does the adjective « bon » usually go?
options: At the end of the sentence
questions.explanation: « Bon » is one of the short common adjectives that precede the noun: « un bon livre ». Its comparative « meilleur » does the same.

questions.stem: How do you say 'my parents' ?
questions.explanation: « Mes » is the plural possessive for both genders, and the noun keeps its own -s. Both halves of the phrase show the plural.

questions.stem: What does « chez » mean in « chez moi »?
questions.explanation: « Chez » means at someone's place — « chez moi », « chez le medecin ». There is no single English word that covers it.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses « depuis » correctly?
options: J'ai habite ici depuis deux ans
Je vais habiter ici depuis deux ans
questions.explanation: « Depuis » with an action still going on takes the present tense in French where English uses 'have been'. The tense mismatch is the whole difficulty.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order in « Je le vois »?
options: The object pronoun goes after the verb
The object pronoun goes at the end
The object pronoun replaces the subject
The object pronoun goes before the verb
questions.explanation: Object pronouns sit in front of the verb in French: « je le vois », 'I see it'. English puts them after, which is why this feels backwards.

questions.stem: What does « y » replace in « J'y vais »?
questions.explanation: « Y » stands in for a place, usually one introduced by « a ». « J'y vais » means I am going there.

questions.stem: Which word means 'and'?
questions.explanation: « Et » is 'and' and « est » is 'is' — one letter apart and constantly confused in writing because they sound different but look similar.

questions.stem: What is the difference between « ou » and « ou » with an accent?
options: One is a question word, the other is plural
One is formal, the other informal
They are spelling variants of one word
One means or, the other means where
questions.explanation: Without the accent it means 'or'; with the grave accent it means 'where'. The accent is the only thing carrying the difference.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'She is a student'?
questions.explanation: With a job or a role after « etre », French drops the article entirely. Adding « une » is the English habit showing through.

questions.stem: How do you say 'the blue cars'?
questions.explanation: Colour adjectives follow the noun and agree with it, so a feminine plural noun gives -es on the adjective too.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'We are going to the shops'?
questions.explanation: « A » plus « les » contracts to « aux » before any plural noun. « Au » is the singular masculine form.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'He does not like the cheese'?
options: Il ne pas aime le fromage
questions.explanation: The definite article survives a negative — only « un », « une », « du » and « des » collapse to « de ». He dislikes that particular cheese.

questions.stem: Why is « Elle est allee » spelled with two e's at the end?
options: The participle agrees with a feminine subject
Every past participle of aller ends in -ee
Aller is irregular in every past tense
The second e marks a plural subject
questions.explanation: Verbs taking « etre » in the perfect agree with the subject, so a feminine subject adds -e and a plural adds -s. Verbs taking « avoir » do not behave this way.

questions.stem: Which is the correct way to say 'it is cold' about the weather?
questions.explanation: Weather takes « faire ». « Il a froid » means he is cold — the person, not the day — and is a perfectly good sentence saying something else.

questions.stem: What is the « nous » form of « etre »?
questions.explanation: « Etre » goes je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous etes, ils sont. It is the most irregular verb in the language and worth learning cold.

questions.stem: What is the « vous » form of « avoir »?
questions.explanation: « Avoir » goes j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont. The « vous » and « nous » forms are the two that look regular.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have been living here for a year'?
options: J'ai habite ici pour un an
Je vais habiter ici depuis un an
questions.explanation: French uses the present with « depuis » for something still true. English reaches for a perfect tense and French does not.

questions.stem: Which of these is an infinitive?
questions.explanation: The infinitive is the dictionary form, ending in -er, -ir or -re. Everything else on this list is already conjugated.

questions.stem: What ending does a regular -er verb take with « ils »?
questions.explanation: « Ils parlent » takes -ent, which is silent. The written form and the spoken form part company here, so it has to be learnt by eye.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'there are a lot of students in the class'?
options: Il y a beaucoup eleves dans la classe
Il y a beaucoup d'eleves dans la classe
Il y a beaucoup des eleves dans la classe
Il y a beaucoup les eleves dans la classe
questions.explanation: Quantity words take plain « de », which shortens to « d' » before a vowel. Two rules stack in one short phrase.
